\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S2-Q11, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=11, type=multi, subtopic={Waves on a string}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: intensity and energy transport of two waves in different media | steps: intensity proportional to density speed omega squared A squared; second wave frequency twice amplitude four times; ratio; check}]
Two waves given by equation $y_1=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$ and $y_2=4A\sin(2\omega t-4kx)$ are traveling in two different strings having same mass per unit length and same cross-sectional area. Tension in first string is four times tension in the second string.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Ratio of average energy density $U_1/U_2$ is $1/64$}
\opt{B}{Ratio of average intensity $I_1/I_2$ is $1/32$}
\opt{C}{Ratio of average power $P_1/P_2$ is $1/16$}
\opt{D}{Ratio of velocity of wave $v_1/v_2$ is $1/2$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Doppler effect}, answer={3}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: beat frequency heard from a source between a man, a wall | steps: direct sound and reflected sound frequencies with the man moving; Doppler shift for both; beat = difference}]
A source of frequency 175 Hz is placed between a man and a wall at the same height of person's ear. Find the velocity $v$ (assume $v\ll c$) of the source with which it should approach the wall such that person will detect 3 beats per second. [Take velocity of sound $c=350$ m/s]
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P2-PHY-S2-Q09, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=2, qno=9, type=multi, subtopic={Standing waves}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: resonance of pipes with hydrogen, helium gases | steps: v = sqrt(gamma R T/M); fundamental frequencies; pipe type; check options}]
Two narrow cylindrical pipes A and B are filled with hydrogen and helium gases respectively at same temperature. Pipe A is open at both ends and pipe B is open at one end and closed at the other end. If frequency of the second overtone of pipe A is equal to the frequency of the first overtone of the pipe B,
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{ratio of the velocities of sound waves in the two pipes $\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}=\sqrt2$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}=\sqrt{\dfrac{42}{25}}$}
\opt{C}{ratio of their lengths $\dfrac{l_A}{l_B}=\sqrt{\dfrac{168}{25}}$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{l_A}{l_B}=2\sqrt2$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=multi, subtopic={Waves on a string}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: speed amplitude, energy of a travelling pulse on a string | steps: y = 2 e^{-(4x^2 + 324 t^2 + 72 x t)} perfect square form; wave moves with speed from ratio of coefficients; mass density and power; check | I: identify a function of x plus vt from a quadratic exponent}, also_in={Nurture SRG - Test 03 (04 Feb 2024) P2 Q8}]
A travelling wave pulse on a string of linear mass density $\dfrac{3\,\mathrm g}{\mathrm{cm}}$ is given by $y=2.00e^{-\left(4x^2+324t^2+72xt+3\right)}$ where x and y are in meter and t in second then choose the correct options.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Wave pulse is travelling along positive x-axis with speed 9 m/s.}
\opt{B}{Wave pulse is travelling along negative x-axis with speed 9 m/s.}
\opt{C}{Tension in the string is 24.3 N}
\opt{D}{Amplitude of wave pulse is 2.00 m}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Waves on a string}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: standing wave from product of cosines: nodes, loop amplitudes | steps: rewrite as sum of travelling waves; wavelength from 20 pi; speed from 100 pi/20 pi; node positions; check}]
A wave disturbance in a medium is described by $y(x,t)=0.08\cos\left(100\pi t+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\cos(20\pi x)$ where x and y are in meter and t in second.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{A node occurs at x = 0.125 m}
\opt{B}{An antinode occurs at x = 0.3 m}
\opt{C}{Speed of component wave is 5 m/s}
\opt{D}{The wavelength is 0.2 m}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Sound waves}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: intensity, amplitude ratio for observers at r and 10r | steps: intensity inverse square so 100:1; amplitude 10:1; loudness difference 20 dB; check statements}]

\opt{D}{If the intensity received by O$_1$ is $10^{-10}\,\dfrac{\mathrm w}{\mathrm m^2}$, the intensity received by O$_2$ will be $10^{-12}\,\dfrac{\mathrm w}{\mathrm m^2}$}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=multi, subtopic={Doppler effect}, answer={A,B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: frequency heard after reflection when the source moves toward a wall | steps: the wall receives Doppler shifted frequency; reflects as source; the source itself hears the echo; beat frequency; check}]
A source emitting a sinusoidal sound wave of frequency 360 Hz travels towards a wall at a speed 30 m/s. What is the beat frequency perceived by an observer moving at speed 10 m/s, speed of sound in air is 330 m/s ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{64Hz if observer is going away from the source and wall.}
\opt{B}{68 Hz if observer is going towards the source and the wall}
\opt{C}{60 Hz if observer is in between the wall and the source and moving away from the wall.}
\opt{D}{24 Hz if observer is in between the wall and the source, and moving towards the wall.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI08-P1-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Waves on a string}, answer={A,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: energy, phase relations for an element of a transverse wave | steps: kinetic energy proportional to particle speed squared; potential energy to slope squared; both equal; maximum at equilibrium; check | I: kinetic and potential energies in phase for a travelling wave}]
A progressive transverse sine wave is passing through a string held along $x$ axis. Consider a small element of the string. Choose the correct statement(s):
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The element executes SHM in a direction perpendicular to $x$ axis.}
\opt{B}{When the element reaches the extreme position, its elastic potential energy is maximum and its kinetic energy is zero.}
\opt{C}{When the element reaches the mean position, its kinetic energy is maximum but its elastic potential energy is zero.}
\opt{D}{At any given instant of time, the kinetic energy and elastic potential energy of the element are the same.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI08-P2-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Standing waves}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: resonance, a tube open at one end driven by a diaphragm | steps: diaphragm is a pressure node? displacement node; so closed end behaves like fixed end; resonant frequencies; check}]
A tube is open at one end and closed at the other by a vibration diaphragm which may be assumed to be a pressure node. It is found that when the frequency of the diaphragm is 2000Hz, a stationary wave pattern is set up in the tube and the distance between adjacent nodes is then 8.0 cm. When the frequency is gradually reduced the stationary wave pattern disappears but another stationary wave pattern reappears at a frequency of 1600 Hz. Neglect end correction.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The speed of sound in air is 320 m/s.}
\opt{B}{The distance between adjacent nodes at a frequency of 1600 Hz is 0.2 m}
\opt{C}{The length of the tube is 40 cm}
\opt{D}{The next lower frequency at which a stationary wave pattern will be obtained is 800 Hz.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P2-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Doppler effect}, answer={A,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: source approaching a pipe open end: resonance condition | steps: Doppler shift of the source frequency; pipe resonance fundamental f0 = v/4L; condition f_s equals harmonic; check}]

The speed of sound in air is $v$ and $f_0$ is the fundamental frequency of the pipe. For which of the following combination(s) of $u$ and $f_s$, will the sound reaching the pipe lead to a resonance ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$u=0.8\,v$ and $f_s=f_0$}
\opt{B}{$u=0.8\,v$ and $f_s=2f_0$}
\opt{C}{$u=0.8\,v$ and $f_s=0.5\,f_0$}
\opt{D}{$u=0.5\,v$ and $f_s=1.5\,f_0$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\opt{B}{If the wind blows from the source to the observer, $f_2>f_1$}

\opt{D}{If the wind blows from the source to the observer, $f_2<f_1$}
\end{qoptions}

\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SII25-P2-PHY-S2-G9-10, source={Score-II - Test 25 (20 Mar 2024)}, questions={9-10}]
Acoustic impedance of a medium is defined as the force per unit layer velocity that a given region applies to an adjacent region, as a wave propagates. Remember that impedance is a property of the medium and not the wave, even though it is generally easiest to calculate it by considering the properties of a travelling wave.

Let us consider a longitudinal progressive wave $s=s_0\sin(\omega t-kx)$.\\
The velocity of a "layer" of molecules whose equilibrium position is $x$ is given by
\[V_P=\frac{\partial s}{\partial t}\]
To find the force, consider a cross-sectional area $A$. We can write the (excess) force that the sheet exerts on the region to its right as
\[F=A\Delta P=-A\left(-B\frac{ds}{dx}\right)\]
And since we are working with a travelling wave we can write.
\[F=\mp A\frac Bv\frac{ds}{dt}\]
where $v$ is velocity of wave and $B$ is bulk modulus of medium.

The force that the sheet feels from the region on its right is the negative of this, but the sign isn't important when calculating the impedance $Z$, because $Z$ is defined to be the magnitude of $\dfrac F{V_P}$, so impedance
\[Z=\frac F{V_P}=\frac{(A)(B)}v=\frac{A\rho v^2}v=A\rho v\]
Where $\rho$ is density of medium.

The impedance per unit area is the more natural thing to talk about, because $Z/A$ is independent of the specific cross section chosen. The force $F$ can be made arbitrarily large by making the area $A$ arbitrarily large, so $Z=F/v$ isn't too meaningful. When people talk about the impedance of air, they usually mean "impedance per area", that is, force per velocity per area. When a sound wave gets reflected from a boundary while going from medium 1 to 2, the amplitudes of reflected and transmitted wave are given by
\[\Delta P_r=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1}\Delta P_i\]
\[\Delta P_t=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}\Delta P_i\]
where $\Delta P_i$ is amplitude of incident wave.
A longitudinal wave goes from medium 1 to medium 2 where $\rho_1v_1=5\times10^6$ kg/m$^2$-s and $\rho_2v_2=45\times10^6$ kg/m$^2$-s, where $\rho$ and $v$ refers to density of medium and wave velocity in the medium.
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SA07-P1-PHY-S2-G7-8, source={Score Advanced - Test 07 (16 Apr 2023)}, questions={7-8}]
If a plane simple harmonic wave is traveling towards positive x axis, its wave function is given by\par
S =S$_0$ sin ($\omega$t -- kx)\par
Here S is longitudinal displacement of any particle. If we take a plane parallel to yz plane all particles in this plane have same phase. This plane is called wavefront.\par
If a plane wave is traveling along direction $\hat{n}$, its wave function can be written as :\par
S = S$_0$ sin ($\omega$t -- k$\hat{n}\cdot\vec{r}$)\par
Let's call k$\hat{n}$ = $\vec{k}$ (a wave vector)\par
S = S$_0$ sin($\omega$t -- $\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}$)\par
Wave vector points in direction of phase velocity. In other words, the wave vector points in the normal direction to the wavefront.\par
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SRG30-P2-PHY-S2-G9-10, source={SRG (Enthusiast) - Test 30 (22 Oct 2023)}, questions={9-10}]
Superposition of waves results in maximum and minimum of intensities such as in case of standing waves. This phenomenon is called as interference. Another type of superposition result in interference in time which is called as beats. In this case waves are analyzed at a fixed point as a function of time. If the two waves are of nearby same frequency are superimposed, at a particular point, intensity of combined waves gives a periodic peak and fall. This phenomenon is beats. If $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are the frequencies of two waves then by superimposed $y=y_1+y_2$ we get at $x=0$,
\[y=\left[2A\cos\left(\frac{\omega_1-\omega_2}{2}\right).t\right]\sin\left[\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}\right].t\]
Thus amplitude frequency is small and fluctuates slowly. A beat i.e., a maximum of intensity occurs, also intensity depends on square of amplitude. The beat frequency is given by\\
$\omega_{\rm beat}=|\omega_1-\omega_2|$\\
Number of beats per second is called as beat frequency. A normal ear can detect only upto 10 Hz of frequency because of persistence of ear.
\end{bankpassage}
